The statement is **true**: $\overline{I\setminus E}=I$.

**Proof.**

Let $I=[0,1]\times[0,1]\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ and let $E\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ have two-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero. We prove the two inclusions separately.

**Inclusion $\overline{I\setminus E}\subseteq I$.**

Since $I\setminus E\subseteq I$ and $I$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^2$, taking closures preserves the inclusion:
$$\overline{I\setminus E}\subseteq \overline{I}=I.$$

**Inclusion $I\subseteq\overline{I\setminus E}$.**

Let $x\in I$ and let $B=B(x,r)$ be any open ball centered at $x$ with $r>0$. To show $x\in\overline{I\setminus E}$ it suffices to show $B\cap(I\setminus E)\neq\varnothing$.

Consider the set $B\cap I$. For every point $x\in I$ (including boundary and corner points), the intersection $B(x,r)\cap I$ contains a nontrivial sector of the ball — at an interior point a full disk, at an edge a half-disk, at a corner a quarter-disk — and in every case
$$m_2\bigl(B(x,r)\cap I\bigr)>0,$$
where $m_2$ denotes two-dimensional Lebesgue measure.

Since $m_2(E)=0$, the set $B(x,r)\cap I$ (which has positive measure) cannot be contained in $E$. Hence there exists a point
$$y\in B(x,r)\cap I\quad\text{with}\quad y\notin E.$$
That is, $y\in B(x,r)\cap(I\setminus E)$, so $B(x,r)\cap(I\setminus E)\neq\varnothing$.

Since this holds for every open ball around $x$, we conclude $x\in\overline{I\setminus E}$. As $x\in I$ was arbitrary,
$$I\subseteq\overline{I\setminus E}.$$

**Conclusion.** Combining both inclusions,
$$\overline{I\setminus E}=I.$$

The key fact used is that a Lebesgue-null set in $\mathbb{R}^2$ has empty interior relative to any region of positive measure, so removing it from $I$ leaves a set dense in $I$.

### PROOF COMPLETE

For the reverse, need I ⊆ closure(I\E). Take any x ∈ I and any open ball B around x. We need B ∩ (I\E) ≠ ∅. Since E has measure zero, B ∩ I is not contained in E (because B∩I has positive measure... wait, B∩I has positive 2D measure if x is interior, but if x is on boundary of I, B∩I still has positive measure).
